opening.headline: The problem of receiving a response as JSON, but the format is broken or the model rejects it, is solved by dividing it into schema constraints and the structure of the rejection response.
body: It's common to fail when trying to parse a model's output in code. Sometimes explanatory sentences are added before and after, essential keys are omitted, and sometimes a rejection phrase appears instead of content. On the surface, they all appear to be parsing failures, but the causes are different.

In this class, we will sequentially look at structured output that constrains the output format by loading the JSON schema into the request, the principles and limitations of constrained decoding guaranteeing the format, the differences in constraints placed on the schema by the three company documents, the structure of the rejection response, and the fallback model. At the end, you'll see an example of how to distinguish between schema violations and safety denials and send them to different processing paths.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain schema constraints and rejection response structure of structured output
You can determine the processing path by distinguishing between schema violations and safety denials.
Explains the principle that constrained decoding guarantees format, and predicts cases where the guarantee is broken.

screens.title: I wanted to receive it as JSON
screens.lead: Read the responses you expected and the three responses you actually received side by side. Although they look similar, it is good to read while thinking about whether the cause is the same.

visual.alt: A scene where the expected JSON and the three actual response cards are placed side by side.
labels: Actual 1: Descriptive sentences before and after
Actual 2: Required key missing or value type mismatch
Reality 3: Only a rejection message arrives without any content

paragraphs: Let's say we're creating a function to extract order information. The expected response is a chunk of JSON containing the name and date. However, the actual response differs in three ways.

First, `JSON.parse` fails because the JSON is preceded or followed by descriptive sentences like "Here are the results." Second, the JSON came, but required keys were missing or the value type was different. Third, only the rejection text is returned instead of the content.

All three failures appear to be parsing errors in your code. But the way to fix it is completely different. The first two are format issues, so they can be solved by restricting the output format, and the third is a policy issue, so no matter how much you refine the format, it cannot be solved. The key to this lesson is to distinguish the causes of failure.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What happens if you retry all three failures the same way? Answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Identifying the causes of failure is the key to this class. First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Recall: the moment parsing broke
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced failure while parsing a model's output in code?
items.answer: If the output format is even slightly shaky, the parser will fail. Since the model is a system that generates sentences, simply asking it to follow the format does not create any guarantees. The structured output covered in this lesson is the function that turns this part into a constraint.

items.prompt: Have you ever strongly written “Print JSON only” in the prompt?
items.answer: Many people try to persevere by changing the wording of the prompt to something stronger. However, since this is only a request, it is sometimes broken, and you have to parse it to find out if it was broken. Schema constraints are a way around this limitation.

items.prompt: How did your code react when the model received a response that simply refused to respond?
items.answer: Most code doesn't allow for rejection. An exception occurs when parsing a response with no content, and the exception is handled in the same way as a format error. Your code should be aware that a rejection is a normal response.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the limitations of the prompt approach, let's take a look at what structured output does.

screens.title: What is structured output?
screens.lead: We break the process of writing structured output into three steps. Select the right arrow to advance through the steps one by one.

visual.alt: Structured output flow diagram with schema, request, and resulting JSON from left to right.

steps.title: 1. Define the schema
steps.body: Write down the desired output shape as a JSON schema. It describes what keys are present, what type the values ​​are, and which keys are required. Gemini can define schemas with Pydantic or Zod, so type definitions in code can be used as schemas.

steps.title: 2. Load schema into request
steps.body: Placing a schema in a request constrains the response to follow that JSON format. Anthropic sends `type: json_schema` to `output_config.format`. To treat tool input strictly, use `strict: true`.

steps.title: 3. Read the response
steps.body: Responses with the schema preserved can be parsed and used immediately. The OpenAI documentation explains that you don't have to worry about missing required keys or getting values ​​that aren't in the enum. Please note that this guarantee applies only if the response completes successfully.

steps.title: 4. Representative uses
steps.body: Structured output is used for data extraction, classification, and tool input generation. This is a case where you need values ​​to be read by code, not text to be read by humans. In this case, it is more stable to restrict it with a schema instead of requesting it with a prompt.

screens.outro: Let's look at how the schema constraints differ across the three companies' documents.

screens.title: Constrained Decoding: Principles and Limitations of Format Guarantees
screens.lead: The table below shows how the schema filters out the next candidate at each moment as the model produces JSON token by token. This is an illustrative example assuming that the schema requires `name` (string) and `age` (integer) and does not allow any other keys. Read from top to bottom.

data.caption: Next tokens filtered by creation location (hypothetical example)
columns: The following tokens accepted by the schema
rows: Curly braces to open an object `{`
The first token of a descriptive sentence like "Here are the results", `[` which opens the array
Fragments of key names `name` and `age` defined in the schema.
Numeric tokens that make up an integer
A string starting with a quote, `null`, a letter
After filling out all required keys
Curly brace `}` to close an object
No more tokens will be picked and generation will stop.
Regardless of filtering, the closing quotes and parentheses are not encountered, so the JSON ends up being left open.
data.notes: Each time the model picks a token, it calculates the probability of the entire vocabulary. Constrained decoding replaces the schema with a grammar rule, sets the probability of a token that violates the rule to 0, and then selects from the remaining candidates. Acceptable candidates vary for each generation location, so they are recalculated for each token. In this principle, three things are explained at once. First, only constraints that can be changed by grammar can be used, so constraints outside the supported range are not applied and are omitted. Second, filtering only works at the moment of selecting a token, so if generation stops in the middle, the result will be unclosed JSON, and the rejection response will also be a normal response that does not follow the schema. Third, what is filtered is only the structure, not the meaning of the value, so the value may be wrong even if the format is correct. The new schema requires preparation for converting the grammar, so the first request may be slow.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principle, let's compare how the three companies' documents specify this constraint and to what extent they support it.

ext.title: OpenAI: Introducing Structured Outputs in the API
Willard, Louf: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models (2023)

screens.title: Differences in Schema Constraints of the Three Companies
screens.lead: Select each tab to check how to specify schema for each company and what to keep in mind. It is good to note that even for the same JSON Schema, the scope of support may vary.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Only some of the standard JSON Schemas are supported, and limited decoding creates valid JSON. When using a schema for the first time, the first request is slow because the grammar is compiled, and the compilation results are cached and reused when using the same schema again. For object, put `additionalProperties: false`. Unsupported constraints, such as `minimum`, are omitted from the sent schema, and the SDK helper transcribes them into the description and verifies the response. Required properties are printed first and optional properties are printed last, so avoid creating code that depends on the order of properties.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: Specify `text.format` with the schemas `type: json_schema` and `strict: true`. The caveat is that if the response is incomplete, it may not satisfy the schema. The documentation explains that in addition to safe rejections, truncated responses due to max tokens may also not conform to the schema. Schema guarantees only apply to normally completed responses.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: Pass JSON Schema to REST. In the SDK, schemas can be defined using Python's Pydantic or JavaScript's Zod, so the model definition in the code can be used as a schema. It supports schema-based structured output, and typical uses include data extraction and classification. Large input documents can be uploaded to the Gemini Files API, referenced in requests, and information extracted from the document can be stored in the schema.

tabs.label: common principles
tabs.body: All three companies use a schema-loading method in the request, and the same point is that schemas within the scope of support must be used. So, keep the schema as simple as possible, and verify unsupported constraints separately in the code. Ensuring that the format is followed and that the values ​​are correct are two separate issues.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen cases where the schema is followed, let's distinguish cases where it fails for formal and other reasons.

screens.title: Structure of rejection response
screens.lead: Below is a simplified example of what a rejection response might look like. When you select a highlighted passage, the meaning of that field appears.

marks.note: In Claude, even if the policy classifier rejects a request, it comes as a normal response rather than an error. So code that only looks at the HTTP status code won't notice the rejection.
This value indicates that the reason the response ended was rejection. You should check this value first before attempting parsing.

stop_details.category tells you which policy area it was rejected for. Keeping records can be used to categorize reasons for rejection and determine responses. In rejections that do not fall into a specific category, the category and explanation may be null, so nulls must also be handled.
This is an explanation of the reason for rejection. Use this as a reference when deciding what guidance to show to users.
Usage is also logged in rejection responses. It can be seen that the response has no content or is short, which is a clue to distinguish it from a format issue.

screens.outro: Let's look at how rejections are subsequently handled, together with the fallback model and the Files API. OpenAI also marks safe rejections separately in the response structure so that the program can detect them.

screens.title: Fallback after rejection: Leave it to the server or implement it yourself?
screens.lead: Compare the method of switching between the two states and leaving the fallback to the server in case of rejection versus implementing it yourself.

visual.alt: Schematic comparing the flow of server-side fallback and direct fallback when a rejection occurs.

states.label: Server-side fallback
states.body: If the classifier for some Claude models rejects a request, you can write a fallback to resend the same request to another model. Server-side fallback is a beta feature. If you send `fallbacks` as `"default"` and the beta header written in the feature document, it will be retried within the same call using Anthropic's recommended model for each rejection category. You can also list models of your own choosing. For categories without a recommended model or for models that do not support fallback, the rejection remains. This simplifies the code, but you still have to deal with getting a rejection response if the fallback doesn't happen.

states.label: Direct fallback
states.body: When implementing it yourself, you create code that detects rejection and calls another model. You can decide which model to pass to, how many times to try, and how to notify the user. Instead, you are responsible for checking and branching to `stop_reason` first. At this time, if you leave the rejected turn in the history and pass it on to another model, it may be rejected again for the same reason, so you must also decide what content to send. Server-side fallback is convenient, but the options are limited, and although implementing it yourself requires some effort, you can tailor the policy to your service.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the tools, let's differentiate between a schema violation and a rejection using a real-world example.

screens.title: Commentary: Two failures that look like the same error
screens.lead: The instructor diagnoses two parsing failure alarms one by one. Select the right arrow to open the diagnostic steps one by one.

visual.alt: A two-line table diagram comparing two parsing failure alerts in terms of symptoms and processing paths.
labels: No schema constraints or out of scope of support
Fallback or user guidance after category recording

steps.title: Take a look at the situation
steps.body: Two parsing failure alerts were raised in the pipeline that extracts order information into JSON. If you look at the logs, both are classified as the same error. First, we start by opening up the reason for terminating the response.

steps.title: Case A: Normal shutdown but no key
steps.body: The response was completed normally, but the required key is missing. This is a clue that the call was made without schema constraints, or that the constraints were not applied because the schema was out of range. It's a format issue.

steps.title: Processing route for case A
steps.body: Check the schema definition and call it again with structured output turned on. If the schema contains unsupported constraints, replace the missing constraints by verifying them in the code.

steps.title: Case B: refusal and no JSON
steps.body: stop_reason is refusal and there is no JSON in content. This is a policy denial, so it has nothing to do with the schema. No matter how much you modify the schema, the same request will be rejected for the same reason.

steps.title: Processing route for case B
steps.body: Note the category of stop_details and retry with a fallback model or branch to inform the user. At this time, it is meaningless to repeat the same request.

steps.title: Summary: If the cause is different, the path is also different.
steps.body: The two alarms looked the same, but the causes were different and the places to fix them were different. Case A fixes the schema, and Case B deals with policy and flow. If you mix the causes, it will happen again even if you fix it.

screens.outro: Let's organize this division into branches of code.

screens.title: Explanation: Organizing processing paths into code branches
screens.lead: The instructor sets up the processing sequence after receiving the response line by line in pseudocode. Select the right arrow to add branches one by one.

steps.title: 1. Look at the reason for termination first
steps.body:
When I receive a response, I check `stop_reason` before parsing it.

```
reason = response.stop_reason
```

If you parse without knowing the reason for termination, any failure will be lumped into a parsing error.

steps.title: 2. If refusal, rejection route
steps.body:
If it's a reject, it doesn't attempt to parse the JSON and sends it to the reject path.

```
if reason == "refusal":
    log(response.stop_details.category)
    return handle_refusal()
```

In the reject path, the category is recorded and divided into fallback model retry or user guidance.

steps.title: 3. Truncated responses increase limits
4. Parsing and verification of normal exit surface
steps.body:
Parse only during normal shutdown. If the SDK has a verification function, even constraints that are not supported and are missing are verified.

```
data = parse(response.text)
validate(data)
```

Correct format and correct value are different, so constraints such as value range are checked at this stage.

steps.title: 5. Record all failures by cause
steps.body: Failures in any path are logged by cause. If you separate out formatting issues, rejections, and truncations and tally them, you'll see a number that shows which areas need improvement. Without this distinction, you won't know why the same alarm is repeated.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: We deal with formal issues and policy issues separately.
screens.lead: Let's go back and organize the first three failure scenes.

paragraphs: The first three failures we see are divided into two format issues and one policy issue. Format issues can be reduced to structured output that constrains the output format by loading a schema into the request, and policy issues arrive as a refusal in stop_reason and must be handled through a separate path.

Rejection comes as a normal response, not an error. So the code must check the reason for termination before parsing, and send rejection, truncation, and graceful termination through different paths. The fallback model and Files API integration are aids in handling two common situations: rejections and large inputs.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Schema guarantees only apply to normally completed responses. Handle rejected or truncated responses separately, regardless of schema.

glossary.def: This function restricts the response to follow the specified JSON schema.
It is a standard format that describes the key, type, and required status of JSON data.
Due to safety policy, the model has declined to respond. In Claude it arrives as stop_reason in the normal response.
This field tells you why the response ended.
This is another model that is called instead in case of rejection or failure.
This method enforces the output structure by excluding tokens that do not conform to the schema from candidates when the model selects tokens one by one.

misconceptions.myth: When structured output is used, any response satisfies the schema.
misconceptions.fact: Schema guarantees do not apply to responses that are rejected or truncated to max tokens. Guarantee is for a properly completed response.

misconceptions.myth: The rejection comes as an HTTP error.
misconceptions.fact: In Claude, this comes as stop_reason in the HTTP 200 OK response. Code that only checks the status code will miss the rejection.

misconceptions.myth: Simply telling the prompt to use JSON is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: Without schema constraints, formatting may be broken, such as adding descriptive sentences or missing keys. Formality must be guaranteed not as a request but as a constraint.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Structured output is a feature that allows you to load a JSON schema into a request so that the response follows that format.
The schema has a limited scope of support, so additionalProperties: false is placed on the object, and some constraints are moved to the description or verified in code.
Because schema violations are formal issues and safety denials are policy issues, they have different causes and responses and are handled through different paths.
The rejection comes as a normal response, not an error, and stop_reason is marked as refusal.
Retry fallback model and Files API integration handle rejection and large input situations.
